body:
## Module 6 in two minutes

201 M6 asked *what may I put into this tool?*: outbound, per workflow, answered deliberately each time. This module runs the other way, and nobody is pasting anything: **what may a system retrieve, on somebody else's behalf, across your whole corpus, forever?**

The mechanism, from the platform's own documentation: the assistant grounds answers in a semantic index over your content and retrieves only what the asking user is permitted to see. **It creates no new access.** That is the vendor's reassurance and it is entirely true.

It is also the whole problem. **The assistant inherits your existing access model, including every mistake in it.** An "anyone with the link" share from 2021. A site widened during a migration and never narrowed. A folder inherited by a team that tripled. Each was a small defensible decision; together they are your actual permission model, and nobody has read it end to end.

> **Every over-share you already had is now one prompt away.**

Which is why the true sentence is useless: *"this is a permissions problem, not an AI problem."* Correct, and it settles nothing. **"AI did not cause this" is true and is not a defence** — the permissions problem was survivable at the old discovery cost and isn't at the new one.

### Summarization launders provenance

Every permission model rests on an assumption nobody wrote down: **that finding something is work.** Three steps stood between a curious person and a document (knowing it existed, knowing where it was, going to get it) and the last one left an audit record.

Retrieval removes the first two. Summarization removes the third. A user asks a general question, gets a good answer, and the answer carries the substance of a document they'd never have opened: **no filename, no permission prompt, no access event, no audit entry.** They didn't read a document. They read an answer.

Three consequences. **Your leak investigation fails**. You go looking for file access and there is none, for anybody. **The user is not culpable in any ordinary sense**, so there's no misconduct to address and therefore no deterrent, which means every control has to be preventive. And the worst one: **aggregation produces facts no document contained.** A calendar, a draft org chart and a budget note can yield who is being managed out. Nobody over-shared that, the assistant assembled it, and it wasn't in anyone's index of sensitive material because it didn't exist until it was asked for.

And your role's specific version: an assistant that can query the HCM can aggregate back to an individual. **"Average salary for the Design team" is a pay disclosure when Design is three people.**

**The full module adds why HR is the worst case, and it's a ratio.** Nowhere else is the proportion of restricted to routine content this high, and worse, **the subjects of your documents are employees with assistant licences.** Elsewhere the sensitive document is about a customer or a deal. Here it's about the person typing the prompt. So generic rollout guidance, sized for a mostly-routine corpus, under-serves you *invisibly*, because nobody involved in the rollout is reading your documents.

Then five moves. Inventory what each assistant indexes as a **separate question** from what your HCM permits. **Exclusion before labelling**, the most reliable protection for a document isn't being in the index, and labelling only protects you to the extent it's correct. **Test as a least-privileged persona, never as yourself**: you're an administrator who can see everything, which makes you the worst possible tester, and the vendor's own guidance says validate per persona. Set a minimum group size on any query interface and **check that it refuses.**

And the one most of you actually need, because you don't own the tenant: **bring the list, not the concern.** You hold the only accurate map of which content is restricted and why — nobody in IT knows that the site called *Project Northstar* holds redundancy selections. A concern gets filed. **Eleven named sites with a sentence each becomes their ten-minute configuration task.**
